sections.h2: Who bills the tax on a Seattle house
sections.html:
King County bills and collects the tax on a Seattle house. The city's own levies ride on the same county statement, so there is no separate city bill. Washington law makes the county treasurer the collector for every district on the roll, whether the levy is for the state, the county, a school district or the city (RCW 84.56.020). The King County Assessor sets the value and publishes the yearly levy sheets that show how Seattle's rate is built.

Seattle counts 784,777 residents (July 1, 2025). Just 43.7% of homes are lived in by their owners, so renters are the majority. Owner-occupied homes had a median value of $938,600 over 2020 to 2024, and households earned a median $123,860.

Seattle's levy code in the King County rate book is 0010. Nearly every parcel inside city limits is in Seattle Public Schools. A small slice of Delridge belongs to the Highline School District instead, which changes the levy lines on the bill.

For 2026 the total levy rate for code 0010 is $9.90845 per $1,000 of assessed value, up from $9.19418 in 2025. The King County Assessor's median-home sheet shows a typical Seattle home assessed at $833,000 for 2026 with a tax of $8,253.74. A year earlier the median assessed value was $864,000 and the tax was $7,943.77.

Across the city, the average assessed value changed by negative 3.6%, the average tax rate changed by 7.8% and the average tax changed by 3.9%, or $309.97. Values slipped while rates rose faster, so the average bill went up.

Voter-approved levies caused the biggest line changes. Seattle School District 1 passed two special levies, a six-year capital levy and a three-year educational technology levy, and its capital line rose from 1.22694 to 1.41465 per $1,000. The city renewed its six-year families, education, preschool and promise levy and a ten-year election campaign voucher levy. The promise line roughly doubled, from 0.34844 to 0.68956.

King County voters renewed several county measures that appear on every Seattle bill:

  • The automated fingerprint identification system levy, a seven-year renewal.
  • The parks, recreation, trails and open space levy, a six-year renewal.
  • The emergency medical services levy, a six-year renewal, with the EMS line moving from 0.22146 to 0.25098.
  • The county-wide hospital line, which went from 0.10000 to 0.15126.

The city lines for low-income housing, library services and the metro park district stayed close to their 2025 levels. If your bill differs from the median figures above, look at which school district and special districts your parcel sits in.

Your Seattle bill splits into two installments. Half is payable by April 30 and the rest by October 31, a schedule set in RCW 84.56.020. Splitting is open to you only when the bill reaches $50. If the second half is still open after October 31, call the King County treasurer for the current balance.

Late taxes on a residence with four or fewer units accrue interest at 9% a year, computed monthly, and state law bars penalties on those homes. Buildings with five or more units are treated harder: 12% a year, a 3% penalty on June 1, and another 8% penalty on December 1. A treasurer may offer payment agreements or accept partial payments, and can extend due dates during a declared state of emergency.

Your statement should reach you by March 15 when the county has the roll in time. If none arrives, ask the King County treasurer for a copy. Not receiving a bill does not cancel the tax.

You petition the county board of equalization on forms approved by the Department of Revenue. Your filing window under RCW 84.40.038 closes on whichever comes later: July 1 of the assessment year, or 30 days after your value notice went out by mail or email. The county may adopt a longer period of up to 60 days, so read the deadline printed on your King County valuation notice.

A board can accept a late petition if you file within a reasonable time and show good cause. The statute lists these circumstances:

  • Death or serious illness of the taxpayer or an immediate family member.
  • Absence from your usual address for more than fifteen of the days allowed.
  • Incorrect written filing advice from board or assessor staff.
  • A natural disaster such as a flood or earthquake.
  • A documented postal delay.

The board must also waive the deadline when your area was revalued, your value did not change, and you were never sent a revaluation notice.

The state senior and disabled exemption, RCW 84.36.381, can excuse part of the excess and regular levies on your home. You need to own the home and live in it. On top of that, one of three things must be true: you turn 61 by December 31 of the filing year, you stopped regular work because of a disability, or you are a veteran rated 40% or higher for a service-connected condition. A surviving spouse or domestic partner of a recipient can qualify at 57 or older. The amount depends on combined disposable income, so ask the King County Assessor for the current income thresholds.

The exemption can move with you. A claimant who sells, transfers or is displaced may carry the exemption status to a replacement residence, though only one residence per year can receive it. Deferred taxes, a separate program under chapter 84.38 RCW, become a lien repaid to the state with interest when ownership transfers. Tell the assessor about your move before the next filing cycle.

A tax lien attaches to the house on January 1 of each levy year. If the sale contract says nothing else, RCW 84.60.020 puts the days before closing on you and the days after on the buyer. Escrow normally settles this at closing, along with any unpaid balance or deferral lien. Get a payoff figure from escrow before you sign anything.

Step by step, a sale with taxes owed goes like this. You list or accept an offer. Escrow orders a title report that shows the unpaid balance. The treasurer's office confirms the amount through the closing date. Escrow pays the balance out of your proceeds and prorates the current year. A cash buyer can skip lender appraisal and underwriting delays, which helps when a deferral lien or back taxes need to be cleared on a short timeline.

sections.h2: Real estate excise tax on a sale
sections.html:
Sellers normally cover the state excise tax on the transfer, payable to the county treasurer when the sale closes. The Department of Revenue brackets for sales from January 1, 2027 climb in four steps: 1.1% through $551,000, 1.28% up to $1,551,000, 2.75% up to $3,051,000, then 3%. A local excise tax comes on top. Ask your closing agent what Seattle's local rate is.

Bring these to the closing office: your most recent tax statement, any exemption or deferral paperwork, the sale agreement and a payoff request from your lender. With those in hand, escrow can show you a full settlement sheet before the day of signing.

faqs.q: What is the Seattle property tax rate for 2026?
faqs.a: The total for levy code 0010 is $9.90845 per $1,000 of assessed value. A median home assessed at $833,000 carries about $8,253.74 in tax.

faqs.q: Does the City of Seattle send its own property tax bill?
faqs.a: No. No. One King County statement covers the city, the school district and every other taxing district, and the county treasurer collects it.

faqs.q: What if the second half is still unpaid after October 31?
faqs.a: Call the King County treasurer for the exact balance. Interest on homes with four or fewer units runs 9% a year, figured monthly, with no penalty.

faqs.q: Can I keep my senior exemption if I sell my Seattle house?
faqs.a: Often yes. You can carry the status to a replacement home, one exempt home per year. Tell the assessor about the move.

faqs.q: Who pays property tax at closing in Seattle?
faqs.a: Unless the contract says otherwise, you owe the days before closing and the buyer owes the days after. Escrow does the math and takes any unpaid balance out of your proceeds.
